SIM, eSIM & pocket Wi-Fi: Korea has fast 5G/LTE almost everywhere – even deep in the subway. Get a prepaid tourist SIM or eSIM (data-only, or with a Korean phone number), or rent a pocket Wi-Fi. The easiest place is the telecom counters (KT, SK telecom, LG U+) in the arrivals hall of Incheon, Gimpo, Gimhae and Jeju airports.
Bring your passport – SIM cards are registered to your name in Korea.
eSIM: order online before you fly and scan the QR code on arrival – your phone must be unlocked and eSIM-compatible.
Pre-ordering online and picking up at the airport counter is often cheaper and skips the queue.
A plan with a Korean number helps when apps or restaurants send a text-message code; data-only plans are cheaper.
Missed the airport? Some convenience stores and telecom shops downtown sell tourist SIMs too, and free "Public WiFi" covers subways, buses and parks.

Airport limousine & intercity buses

Airport limousine buses go from the airport straight to hotel areas and other cities. Find your destination on the route board in the arrivals hall, buy a ticket at the counter or kiosk (many routes also take a transit card or bank card), and wait at the stop number shown on your ticket – staff load your suitcase under the bus.
Paying by card: tap once when you get on. On city buses also tap when you get off – that gives the free transfer.
Getting off: the next stop is announced in Korean and English and shown on the screen. Press the STOP button before your stop and follow the route in a map app.
Tell the driver or the luggage staff your hotel or stop when you board – they often call it out for you.
Intercity buses (고속·시외버스) leave from bus terminals: buy at the kiosk or app, sit in the seat on your ticket, and note the bus number at rest stops.

Subway: express trains, riding & announcements

Tap your transit card at the gate, find the platform by the line colour and the direction sign ("…방면" = towards …), and tap again at the exit gate – the fare depends on the distance. Trains run about every 3–10 minutes from roughly 5:30 until around midnight.
Express (급행, often shown in red) skips stations; local (일반) stops everywhere. Line 9 and several suburban lines have both – check the sign on the train and the platform screen.
Door numbers like 3-2 (car 3, door 2) are painted on the platform; map apps tell you the best door for a quick transfer or exit.

Announcements give the next station, transfer lines and which side the doors open, in Korean and English (plus Chinese and Japanese on many lines). A short traditional tune plays before transfer stations.
Rush hours (about 7:30–9:00 and 18:00–19:30) are packed – travel with big suitcases outside these times. Check the last train in your app.
Wrong gate or card problem? Press the help button at the gate; lost items go to the station office.

Public toilets & bidets
Korea has plenty of free, clean public toilets – in subway stations, parks, tourist sites, department stores and highway rest areas. Look for the 화장실 (toilet) sign.
Toilet paper goes into the toilet – most public toilets have no paper bin any more. Only sanitary products go in the small bin.
Bidet buttons: 세정 = rear wash, 비데 = front wash, 건조 = dry, 정지 (often red ■) = stop. Press stop before you stand up!
Wait in one line at the entrance, not in front of a single stall, and knock lightly before opening a door.
Older markets and rural toilets may lack paper or have a squat toilet (face the hooded end) – carry tissues.
Many public toilets have an emergency bell (비상벨) that calls security or the police.
Ordering at restaurants & kiosks

In most local restaurants you just sit down. Water and side dishes are free. Call the staff with the bell on the table or "저기요!", order, and pay at the counter on your way out. Many places now use a table tablet, a QR code or a kiosk instead.
Kiosk steps: language button (often top-right) → menu → options (size, spice, hot/iced) → 매장 eat in / 포장 take out → pay (card in the slot, chip first) → keep the receipt with your number.
When your number appears on the screen (or the buzzer rings), pick up the food at the counter.
Some dishes are for 2 or more people (2인분 이상), e.g. BBQ and stews – solo travellers look for 1인분 or 혼밥 places.
No tipping – menu prices include tax. Water, cutlery and refills are often at the self-service corner (셀프).
